newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Arafat calls conference on crisis in peace moves.
newsitem.headline: Arafat calls conference on crisis in peace moves.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat sought on Tuesday to draw the United States deeper into salvaging Middle East peace talks that have foundered on Israeli settlement plans in the West Bank.

The PLO chairman invited U.S., European and Arab envoys to a meeting on Saturday to discuss a crisis brewing since Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu approved plans to build Jewish housing between Arab East Jerusalem and Bethlehem.

But Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy, in a hastily convened news conference, said such a meeting would violate agreements and warned that PLO efforts to bring international pressure on Israel could freeze peace moves.

"Any appeal which could bring about international involvement could -- and I am warning that such a danger exists even if Israel does not want it to come about -- bring about a freeze in the political process," Levy told reporters.
He called on the countries not to participate.
Jordan's King Hussein, the Arab leader closest to Netanyahu, warned the Israeli prime minister of an "explosion of the peace process" unless the settlement plan was dropped.

Arafat, feeling the frustration of the Palestinian street and of his own PLO colleagues, has tried to rally support at the United Nations and among Western and Moslem countries for halting the settlement.
The crisis deepened last Friday when Israel disclosed the depth of the first of three West Bank pullbacks. It offered the Palestinians about a third of what they wanted.

Underscoring tensions, an Israeli soldier guarding a West Bank Jewish settlement near Hebron was stabbed 20 times and wounded seriously in an apparent Palestinian guerrilla attack, military sources said on Tuesday. The two attackers fled with his gun.

Levy said Arafat's move was an attempt to wring greater territorial concessions from Israel in the next two West Bank redeployments, which must be completed by mid-1998 under peace deals with the PLO.
"No one should be enticed into thinking that by doing so they will be able to pressure Israel to act against its will and interests," said Levy.
Saeb Erekat, a Palestinian negotiator, said Arafat had invited representatives from the United States, Russia, the European Union, Egypt, Jordan, Japan and Norway to the meeting.
"This is the pattern he has followed in the past," said an Israeli government official. "He wants the U.S. in deeper."
Western officials said the United States was already actively engaged in the four-year-old Oslo process and doubted it would do significantly more.

They said they were concerned by the depth of distrust between Israelis and Palestinians. But they echoed the assessment of Israeli security sources that the kind of violence seen during the last crisis in September was not yet on the cards. Sixty-one Palestinians and 15 Israeli soldiers died in gun battles then.
"Arafat is in full control of the Palestinian areas. If he wants to keep this crisis off the streets he can," said one Israeli security official.
Netanyahu, on a visit to Moscow, defended his settlement plan and criticised "doomsday" talk.

"We have disagreements. We cannot at every stage of this agreement engage in cataclysmic predictions and talk of crisis and violence," Netanyahu told a news conference. Several Netanyahu aides did not travel to Moscow because of the crisis.
Arafat has refused more than twice since Friday to receive Netanyahu's representatives who wanted to explain the decision to hand over nine percent of the rural West Bank, a PLO official said.

Arafat's chief negotiator Mahmoud Abbas, better know as Abu Mazen, has tendered his resignation from the negotiating team in protest at the Israeli offer. Arafat has not yet said whether he will accept it.
Israeli officials called the resignation a ploy. Western officials noted that Abu Mazen was one of the more moderate negotiators who had a good handle on the Israeli domestic political scene.

"We have told the Israelis they need to be careful. Abu Mazen is the person they have found to be the most moderate...Maybe he feels he has been burned by the Israelis once too often," one Western official said.
